kakekotoba.reading_secondary: みな ("all/everyone") — associative pun, though primarily functioning as jokotoba pivot
kakekotoba.interaction: The river name Minano-gawa is introduced literally as the river formed from Tsukuba's peaks, but its component sound みな also faintly echoes 皆 ("all/everything"), reinforcing the sense of totality/accumulation carried into 恋ぞつもりて — however this is a soft, secondary resonance rather than a fully split grammatical pivot, so it is noted but the primary device here is jokotoba, not a strict kakekotoba

jokotoba.text: 筑波嶺の峰より落つるみなの川
jokotoba.pivot: みな(の川)→淵(となりぬる)
jokotoba.function: The entire kami-no-ku describes the physical formation of the Minano River, cascading from the peaks of Mt. Tsukuba and gradually deepening into a pool (淵). This composed, poem-specific image is not a fixed epithet but a freely built preface whose logic (small stream becoming a deep pool) is transferred by structural analogy onto the shimo-no-ku's claim that accumulated longing has become a deep pool of love. The pivot is essentially the shared image of gradual accumulation culminating in 淵 (a deep pool), mapped onto つもりて (accumulating) and 淵となりぬる (has become a deep pool).

honkadori.source_poem: Man'yōshū-derived commonplace on Tsukuba/Minano-gawa (also echoed in later waka tradition, e.g. Gosenshū anonymous poems on Mt. Tsukuba's waters)
honkadori.echoed_phrase: 筑波嶺の峰より落つるみなの川
honkadori.function: Invokes the well-established poetic association of Mt. Tsukuba's cascading streams converging into the Minano (or Sakura) River as a conventional emblem of small beginnings growing into overwhelming force, lending the poem's central metaphor an air of received, authoritative imagery rather than pure invention.

kigo.note: Mt. Tsukuba and the Minano River are famous utamakura (poetic place-names) but carry no fixed seasonal association in the classical canon — they function here as topographical/rhetorical material for the jokotoba rather than as a seasonal marker. No other lexical item in the poem (峰, 落つる, 恋, つもりて, 淵) carries seasonal connotation either; 恋 (love) is a perennial topic-category (koi-uta) rather than a seasonal one. After exhaustive check of every noun and verb, this poem is best classified as non-seasonal, belonging to the love (恋) section of the anthology rather than any seasonal book.

bipartite.kami_theme: A small stream cascading down from the peaks of Mt. Tsukuba, gradually gathering into the Minano River
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker's love, accumulating over time, has become a deep, unfathomable pool of emotion
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku's physical description of trickling mountain water accumulating into a deep pool (淵) is never explicitly compared to the speaker's love — the shimo-no-ku simply asserts that 'love has piled up and become a pool,' relying entirely on the reader recognizing the sustained river-image of the kami as the vehicle for the tenor of accumulated passion. The word 淵 functions as the hinge: literal deep pool in the river, and metaphorical depth of overwhelming love, uniting both halves without any explicit comparative particle.
